title: Psychosocial impact of Marburg virus disease on recovered individuals and frontline health workers in Rwanda: a cross-sectional survey.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To examine the psychosocial impact of this disease on recovered individuals and frontline health workers (FHWs) following the 2024 MVD outbreak in Rwanda. DESIGN: a cross-sectional survey. SETTING: Kigali, the capital city of Rwanda, had two treatment centres during the outbreak of the MVD disease from 24 September to 24 October 2024. PARTICIPANTS: All 51 recovered individuals from MVD and 98 FHWs who met the eligibility criteria were involved in the study.Depression was measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), anxiety with the Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) scale and post-traumatic stress disorder using the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5). Perceived stigma was measured using the adapted Ebola stigma and discrimination questionnaire and the Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support Scale (MPSS) to assess social support. Wilcoxon rank-sum and Kruskal-Wallis tests examined differences in depression, anxiety and PTSD by sex and profession. Spearman correlation assessed relationships between variables. RESULTS: 115 participants, including 29 recovered people and 86 FHWs. 11.8% of FHWs had moderate to severe depression and 20.7% of recovered people had mild to moderate depression. Moderate to severe anxiety was exhibited by 9.4% of FHWs, and mild anxiety was reported by 17.2% of recovered people. 9.3% of FHWs and one recovered individual had a total PCL score above 33 (PTSD). Among recovered people, there was a significant negative correlation between anxiety and social support (r=-0.36, p value=0.05) and a significant difference in PTSD symptom levels between sexes (p value=0.01). Among FHWs, MVD-related stigma was positively correlated with PTSD symptoms (r=+0.23, p value=0.05). Symptoms of depression (β coef.=-0.19, 95% CI -0.32, -0.05) and anxiety (β coef.=-0.16, 95% CI -0.26, -0.06) decreased with age. Married FHWs had lower levels of depression (β coef.=-2.72, 95% CI -4.96, -0.49) and anxiety (β coef.=-2.35, 95% CI -4.07, -0.62) compared with single individuals. CONCLUSION: Six months post-containment of the MVD outbreak in Rwanda, many FHWs were still experiencing depression, anxiety and PTSD. Contextualised and culturally adapted mental health and psychosocial support interventions are highly recommended for integration into infectious disease response plans.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在探讨2024年MVD 暴发后,马尔堡病毒病对卢旺达康复者及一线医护人员的心理社会影响。研究动机源于了解该疾病对受影响人群心理健康后果的必要性。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 在卢旺达首都基加利进行了一项横断面调查,该城市在2024年9月24日至10月24日的MVD 暴发期间设有两个治疗中心。所有符合纳入标准的51名MVD康复者和98名一线医护人员均被纳入研究。
elements_zh.methods: 使用患者健康问卷(PHQ-9)评估抑郁,使用广泛性焦虑障碍量表(GAD-7)评估焦虑,使用DSM-5创伤后应激障碍检查清单(PCL-5)评估创伤后应激障碍(PTSD)。使用改编版埃博拉病毒污名与歧视问卷评估感知污名,使用多维社会支持感知量表(MPSS)评估社会支持。
elements_zh.main_results: 研究共纳入115名参与者,包括29名康复者和86名一线医护人员。在一线医护人员中,11.8%有中度至重度抑郁,20.7%的康复者有轻度至中度抑郁。9.4%的一线医护人员报告有中度至重度焦虑,而17.2%的康复者有轻度焦虑。1名康复者和9.3%的一线医护人员总PCL评分超过33分,表明存在PTSD。在康复者中,焦虑与社会支持之间存在显著负相关(r=-0.36,p值=0.05),且性别间PTSD症状水平存在显著差异(p值=0.01)。在一线医护人员中,与MVD相关的污名与PTSD症状呈显著正相关(r=+0.23,p值=0.05)。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者得出结论,卢旺达MVD 暴发被控制六个月后,许多一线医护人员仍经历抑郁、焦虑和PTSD。他们强调了研究的新颖性,即关注马尔堡病毒病对康复者和医护人员的心理社会影响。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,应将心理健康和心理社会支持干预措施纳入传染病应对计划,以应对受影响个体和医护人员持续的心理负担。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性在于其横断面设计,无法进行因果推断。由于依赖自我报告测量和调查环境中的潜在偏倚,证据强度中等。

analysis_zh.main_results: 研究共纳入115名参与者,包括29名康复者和86名一线医护人员。在一线医护人员中,11.8%有中度至重度抑郁,20.7%的康复者有轻度至中度抑郁。9.4%的一线医护人员报告有中度至重度焦虑,而17.2%的康复者有轻度焦虑。1名康复者和9.3%的一线医护人员总PCL评分超过33分,表明存在PTSD。在康复者中,焦虑与社会支持之间存在显著负相关(r=-0.36,p值=0.05),且性别间PTSD症状水平存在显著差异(p值=0.01)。在一线医护人员中,与MVD相关的污名与PTSD症状呈显著正相关(r=+0.23,p值=0.05)。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者得出结论,卢旺达MVD 暴发被控制六个月后,许多一线医护人员仍经历抑郁、焦虑和PTSD。他们强调了研究的新颖性,即关注马尔堡病毒病对康复者和医护人员的心理社会影响。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,应将心理健康和心理社会支持干预措施纳入传染病应对计划,以应对受影响个体和医护人员持续的心理负担。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性在于其横断面设计,无法进行因果推断。由于依赖自我报告测量和调查环境中的潜在偏倚,证据强度中等。

title: Machine learning-enhanced stochastic modeling of Marburg virus transmission in human–bat populations
abstract: A serious threat to global health is the Marburg virus, which affects human beings as well as non-human primates. This study develops a comprehensive stochastic mathematical model to examine Marburg virus transmission dynamics in human and bat populations, incorporating vaccination effects and random environmental factors including immigration, climate change, and behavioral variations. In this work, we employ stochastic differential equations coupled with neural network analysis to capture the complex disease dynamics. First, we prove that the solution exists globally and is positive. Next, we establish the fundamental stochastic reproduction number, which serves as a threshold parameter determining disease extinction ( R 0 s 1 ) in the population. Numerical simulation is performed to investigate the dynamics of Marburg virus disease in the population. Numerical simulation shows that as value of vaccination increases, it leads to decreases in the spread of Marburg virus. This shows that vaccination is very important to control the spread of Marburg virus in the community. A feedforward neural network (FFNN) is employed as a surrogate model and trained using the numerical solution generated by the Euler–Maruyama scheme. The network learns a continuous nonlinear mapping from simulation time to the corresponding compartmental states, thereby providing a smooth approximation of the realized stochastic trajectory. The simulated dataset is randomly divided into training (70%), validation (15%), and testing (15%) subsets. The accuracy of Neural Networks in prediction and modeling is demonstrated by dividing the data into 70% for training, 15% for testing, and 15% for validation. Validating its accuracy, the model attains a mean squared error of 2.39 × 10−4 averaged over the eight compartments and a regression coefficient close to one (R = 0.999). The results of this study offer public health strategists effective tools for reducing or eliminating Marburg virus.

title: Lethal Sudan virus infection in IFNAR-/- mice is characterized by key inflammatory features of filovirus disease.
abstract: Sudan virus (SUDV) is a member of the family Filoviridae , which comprises highly pathogenic viruses associated with unusually high case fatality rates. The development of medical countermeasures against filoviruses, including antivirals, vaccines, and therapeutic antibodies, requires preclinical evaluation in suitable animal models. C57BL/6J IFNAR -/- mice, which lack the type I interferon (IFN-α/β) receptor, have been reported to be susceptible to filovirus infections, although their impaired innate immune response may represent a potential limitation of the model. Here, we characterized the clinical, virological, pathological, and inflammatory responses following SUDV Boniface infection in IFNAR -/- mice. Following infection, animals developed progressive clinical disease characterized by substantial weight loss and pronounced changes in behavior and appearance. Mice reached the predefined clinical endpoint 3–5 days post infection. Post mortem analysis of terminal samples revealed high viral loads and viral genome copies in all tested organs as well as in serum, consistent with widespread systemic dissemination. Histopathological examination revealed prominent lesions, particularly in the liver and spleen. In addition, terminal serum analysis revealed a broad and pronounced inflammatory response, with significantly elevated concentrations of multiple cytokines and chemokines compared with non-infected controls, encompassing pro-inflammatory, regulatory, and hematopoietic mediators. Together, these findings characterize the clinical course, systemic viral dissemination, tissue pathology, and terminal inflammatory response associated with lethal SUDV infection in IFNAR -/- mice. The observed cytokine and chemokine elevations are consistent with inflammatory responses described in filovirus infections, although the single terminal sampling time point and limited cohort size preclude conclusions regarding the temporal development or mechanistic basis of this response. These data support the utility of this model for investigating filovirus pathogenesis and infection-associated immune responses and warrant further evaluation of its suitability for SUDV infection and for preclinical studies of filovirus countermeasures.

title: Proteomic comparison of Marburg and Kasokero virus infection in natural host Egyptian rousette bat reveals distinct antiviral pathways
abstract: Abstract Bats are natural reservoir hosts for numerous zoonotic viruses, yet the molecular mechanisms enabling viral persistence without overt disease remain incompletely understood. The Egyptian rousette bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus, ERB) is the sole known natural reservoir of Marburg virus (MARV) and a key host in the enzootic cycle of the tick-borne Kasokero virus (KASV), providing a unique system to compare host responses to different RNA viruses within the same species. Here, we applied serial cross-sectional serum proteomics integrated with tissue-specific viral kinetics to characterize systemic host responses to experimental MARV and KASV infection in captive-reared bats. Nearly 16 % of detected proteins (67/419) were found exclusively in infected animals, yet canonical acute inflammatory signatures driving pathology in other susceptible hosts were absent (e.g., in humans and non-human primates). Differential abundance and detection analyses identified both shared and virus-dependent responses, with MARV infection eliciting limited and transient perturbations, while KASV induced broader and more sustained engagement of complement, lectin pathway, and hepatometabolic proteins. Network-based analysis uncovered coordinated proteasome modules — including circulating immunoproteasome complexes — consistent with enhanced antigen-processing capacity is a feature of these virus-host dynamics. Together, these findings reveal how ERBs mount structured, virus-dependent systemic responses, offering new insight into mechanisms underlying viral infection in natural reservoir hosts.

title: Ebola virus disease through the one health lens: Integrating human, animal and environmental health for preparedness, prevention, and control – A narrative review
abstract: Ebola virus disease (EVD) is a severe, often fatal zoonotic disease that continues to pose a serious public health challenge, especially in Central and West Africa. Despite major progress in diagnostics, infection prevention, vaccination, and therapeutics, Ebola outbreaks repeatedly reveal gaps in surveillance, preparedness, ecological risk monitoring, and community trust. The disease is not driven by the virus alone; its emergence and spread are shaped by interactions between wildlife reservoirs, environmental change, sociocultural practices, population movement, and fragile health systems. Viewing EVD through a One Health lens helps in understanding these connections more clearly. Human health, animal health and ecosystem health are closely linked, and Ebola prevention cannot depend only on clinical care after cases appear. Effective control requires early detection of human illness, monitoring of wildlife and ecological risks, strong laboratory systems, infection prevention in health facilities, timely treatment, safe and dignified burial practices, vaccination where applicable and meaningful community engagement. Risk communication must be based on trust, respect and local participation, particularly in communities where caregiving and funeral practices are deeply rooted in social and cultural life. Although recent advances have improved the outlook for Ebola control, important challenges remain. Weak intersectoral coordination, inadequate financing, limited veterinary public health capacity, insecurity, fragmented data systems and low community confidence continue to affect preparedness and response. Strengthening One Health platforms at local, national and global levels is therefore essential, not only for EVD, but also for future emerging and re-emerging zoonotic diseases in a rapidly changing global landscape.

title: EMERGENT AND RE-EMERGENT ZOONOTIC THREATS: CURRENT STATUS, CHALLENGES AND COUNTERACTION STRATEGIES
abstract: The modern world is characterized by the globalization of most processes, accompanied by the speed and scale of change. Over the past 30 years, more than 30 new human pathogens have been identified, 75% of which originated in animals. The emergence of new zoonotic diseases and the resurgence of well-known ones remain a significant challenge for the public health system. The aim of this study is to analyze the current status of emerging and re-emerging zoonotic threats, their epidemic potential, and the necessary countermeasures at the global and national levels. Materials and Methods. An analysis was conducted of official WHO reports (Disease Outbreak News, 2025– July 2026), data from the Global Influenza Surveillance System, and scientific publications in the PubMed and Scopus databases for the period 2016–2026. The bibliosemantic method and descriptive statistics were used. Results and Discussion. Data on current zoonotic infections, including «Disease X» were summarized. The relevance of the issue was demonstrated using the example of outbreaks and epidemics with high mortality rates from 2025 to July 2026. (Marburg disease in Tanzania — 100%, Ebola in the DRC — 70.3%, Nipah disease in Bangladesh — 100%, etc.). The trend in human cases of zoonotic influenza shows an increase in the number of infections with A(H5N1) viruses and the emergence of new viral subtypes (A(H5N5), A(H5N2), A(H9N2)) that are emerging in humans. The need to further implement the «One Health» concept and strengthen national biosafety systems, taking pandemic preparedness into account, has been substantiated. Emerging zoonotic threats remain a priority area for global public health. Effective countermeasures are possible only through strengthened epidemiological surveillance, the development of new diagnostic, therapeutic, and preventive measures, the implementation of the «One Health» approach at the national level, and international cooperation, particularly within the framework of the 2025 Pandemic Prevention Agreement. Keywords: emergent infections, re-emergent zoonoses, «Disease X», avian influenza, biosecurity, «One Health», pandemic preparedness.

title_zh: 新兴和再发的人兽共患病威胁:现状、挑战与应对策略
source_body_en: The modern world is characterized by the globalization of most processes, accompanied by the speed and scale of change. Over the past 30 years, more than 30 new human pathogens have been identified, 75% of which originated in animals. The emergence of new zoonotic diseases and the resurgence of well-known ones remain a significant challenge for the public health system. The aim of this study is to analyze the current status of emerging and re-emerging zoonotic threats, their epidemic potential, and the necessary countermeasures at the global and national levels. Materials and Methods. An analysis was conducted of official WHO reports (Disease Outbreak News, 2025– July 2026), data from the Global Influenza Surveillance System, and scientific publications in the PubMed and Scopus databases for the period 2016–2026. The bibliosemantic method and descriptive statistics were used. Results and Discussion. Data on current zoonotic infections, including «Disease X» were summarized. The relevance of the issue was demonstrated using the example of outbreaks and epidemics with high mortality rates from 2025 to July 2026. (Marburg disease in Tanzania — 100%, Ebola in the DRC — 70.3%, Nipah disease in Bangladesh — 100%, etc.). The trend in human cases of zoonotic influenza shows an increase in the number of infections with A(H5N1) viruses and the emergence of new viral subtypes (A(H5N5), A(H5N2), A(H9N2)) that are emerging in humans. The need to further implement the «One Health» concept and strengthen national biosafety systems, taking pandemic preparedness into account, has been substantiated. Emerging zoonotic threats remain a priority area for global public health. Effective countermeasures are possible only through strengthened epidemiological surveillance, the development of new diagnostic, therapeutic, and preventive measures, the implementation of the «One Health» approach at the national level, and international cooperation, particularly within the framework of the 2025 Pandemic Prevention Agreement. Keywords: emergent infections, re-emergent zoonoses, «Disease X», avian influenza, biosecurity, «One Health», pandemic preparedness.

title: VSV-EBOV vaccination induces cross-reactive T-cell responses against Bundibugyo virus in humans
abstract: Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV) is causing an ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) with no licensed vaccine available. Recent reports have shown the presence of BDBV-cross-reactive antibody responses in humans vaccinated against the related Ebola virus (EBOV). Here, we used an IFN-γ ELISpot assay to assess T cell responses against the EBOV, BDBV and SUDV glycoproteins in clinical trial participants vaccinated with the licensed VSV-EBOV vaccine. We could show that BDBV-cross-reactive T cell responses are detectable in the majority of individuals and that conserved regions within the glycoprotein are targeted. In the absence of a BDBV-specific vaccine, these data support efficacy trials of the VSV-EBOV vaccine during the current outbreak.

title: Knowledge graph and machine learning-guided virtual screening prioritizes putative blockers of the PSMD11/Rpn6-EBOV glycoprotein interface
abstract: Introduction Host-directed antiviral discovery requires a traceable route from host-factor identification to testable molecular hypotheses. This study developed such a workflow around a host factor associated with Ebola virus glycoprotein (EBOV GP). Methods GFP-GP pulldown coupled with co-immunoprecipitation/mass spectrometry was used to identify GP-associated host candidates. A PSMD11/Rpn6-centred workflow integrated knowledge-graph inference, ligand-only machine learning, ADMETlab profiling and interface-guided docking. Candidate prioritization was assessed through score-weight sensitivity analysis, applicability-domain assessment and docking controls addressing seed reproducibility, search convergence, whole-receptor context and macrocycle ring-conformer sensitivity. Docking scores were contextualized against a matched 59-compound library. Results The analysis recovered 424 GP-pulldown-specific host proteins and nominated PSMD11/Rpn6 as a proteostasis anchor. The tier-gated knowledge-graph candidate membership was invariant across the tested weight perturbations, with Spearman rho = 0.998 under equal weighting. The selected ExtraTrees model achieved an AUC of 0.912 for the Ki endpoint. Applicability-domain assessment and ADMET profiling differentiated candidate confidence and predicted liabilities. Docking reproducibility checks yielded a maximum standard deviation of 0.05 kcal/mol for conformationally restricted ligands, while macrocyclic candidates showed greater protocol-dependent variability. Rule-based triage integrating upstream evidence, ADMET burden, chemotype diversity and mechanistic coverage returned five candidates: betamethasone, bafilomycin A1, everolimus, pitavastatin and CHEMBL1410015. Discussion The workflow links a proteomic host-factor signal to a compact set of chemically diverse hypotheses with explicit evidence sources and limitations. The candidates remain hypotheses for experimental assessment; direct target engagement, interface blockade and antiviral activity are not established by the present study.

Introduction The resurgence of viral haemorrhagic fevers across Africa underscores the fragility of global health security and the persistent ethical vulnerabilities facing frontline healthcare workers. Recurrent outbreaks of Ebola virus disease in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Uganda, alongside Marburg virus disease alerts in several African countries, show how rapidly localised epidemics can become regional and international public health threats.1 2 These crises reveal that high-consequence infectious disease outbreaks are not isolated national emergencies. They are interconnected global health challenges that expose structural inequities in preparedness, response and health system resilience.3 4These vulnerabilities are unfolding within a shifting international political and economic order. The move from aid-centred global health engagement towards the growing ‘prominence of trade objectives’ occurs in an increasingly fragmented geopolitical environment.5 While such transitions may create opportunities for economic advancement, they also risk deepening the vulnerability of health systems already strained by historical underinvestment, debt burdens, workforce shortages and uneven infrastructure development.6 Under these conditions, epidemic response capacity cannot be separated from broader questions of global justice and the distribution of institutional resilience.Recent Ebola outbreaks in the DRC and Uganda, together with recurring Marburg virus disease threats, continue to expose ethical and structural weaknesses in post-COVID-19 health systems. Even outbreaks that remain relatively contained impose substantial moral and occupational burdens on healthcare workers operating within fragile institutions.7 Across recurrent epidemics, the foundational pillars of resilient health systems—workforce capacity, infection prevention infrastructure, essential medicines, financing, governance and community trust—remain uneven and often inadequate.8 9Frontline healthcare workers are therefore required to navigate competing obligations to patients, families, colleagues, communities and themselves while often lacking adequate institutional protection. The ethical dilemmas they face extend beyond clinical decision-making. They include questions of professional duty amid personal risk, justice in resource allocation, reciprocity between institutions and workers, community trust and the psychological consequences of sustained moral distress.7 10 These challenges are amplified in contexts where historical neglect, underinvestment and inequitable global responses have eroded confidence in public institutions.This commentary argues that ethical preparedness must become a central component of epidemic response. Without transparent decision-making processes, reciprocal institutional support, and meaningful community engagement, outbreak responses risk collapsing under the weight of moral uncertainty, endangering both healthcare workers and the populations they serve. Ethical preparedness and the limits of the duty to careEmerging infectious disease outbreaks expose a fundamental tension within healthcare professionalism: the expectation that healthcare workers will continue delivering care despite substantial personal risk. During outbreaks of highly infectious diseases, frontline healthcare workers are expected to uphold beneficence while facing threats to their own safety, their families and their communities. Yet the ethical legitimacy of this expectation depends on whether institutions and governments fulfil reciprocal obligations to protect them.In many low-resource settings, this reciprocity remains incomplete. Personal protective equipment, infection prevention infrastructure, laboratory capacity, workforce surge mechanisms and occupational protections are often insufficient during epidemic escalation. Under such conditions, the duty to care risks becoming less a professional obligation grounded in mutual trust and more a form of institutionalised sacrifice.11 The ethical question is therefore not simply whether healthcare workers should respond during outbreaks, but whether health systems have done enough to justify asking them to assume extraordinary risks.During Ebola outbreaks in West Africa and the DRC, frontline healthcare workers experienced disproportionate infection and mortality, reflecting systemic failures in preparedness rather than individual shortcomings. Similar patterns emerged during COVID-19, when health systems worldwide relied on professional altruism to compensate for chronic underinvestment in workforce protection. The repeated normalisation of healthcare worker sacrifice reveals a dangerous assumption within global health governance: that resilience can substitute for structural support.Ethical preparedness must therefore be understood as a core pillar of epidemic preparedness. Protecting healthcare workers requires more than emergency procurement once crises begin. It demands sustained investment in workforce safety, fair compensation, mental health services, safe working conditions, transparent institutional accountability and mechanisms for worker participation in planning and response. Without these safeguards, healthcare workers are left to absorb the moral and physical costs of systemic fragility. Resource allocation, structural inequity and procedural justiceOutbreak settings frequently force healthcare workers to make decisions under profound scarcity. In fragile health systems, triage extends beyond clinical prioritisation and becomes a reflection of deeper structural inequities. Decisions about access to isolation units, supportive therapies, referral pathways, diagnostics and critical care resources are often shaped by geography, socioeconomic status, infrastructure and political marginalisation rather than clinical need alone.The ethical principle of justice requires that scarce resources be allocated fairly and transparently.12 However, operationalising justice during epidemics is especially difficult where baseline inequities already shape health outcomes. Patients from remote or underserved communities may present later because of transportation barriers, mistrust, delayed surveillance or weak referral systems. As a result, they may appear clinically ‘less likely’ to survive. Strict utilitarian frameworks that prioritise those with the highest probability of survival may therefore systematically disadvantage populations already excluded from equitable healthcare access.These dilemmas show why ethical decision-making during outbreaks cannot rely solely on abstract triage principles imported from high-resource settings. Ethical frameworks must account for the historical and structural conditions that shape vulnerability. Procedural justice is essential. This includes transparent triage criteria, multidisciplinary decision-making, documentation of decisions, appeals processes where feasible, and community-informed accountability mechanisms.13Frontline healthcare workers often shoulder these decisions without adequate institutional guidance. The psychological burden of repeated moral compromise contributes to burnout, moral injury and long-term workforce attrition. Ethical preparedness therefore requires not only technical triage protocols but also systems that distribute responsibility collectively rather than leaving individual providers isolated in impossible decision-making environments. Community trust as a foundation of epidemic responseOutbreak control depends not only on biomedical interventions but also on public trust. Experiences from Ebola and COVID-19 responses show that containment measures imposed without meaningful community engagement can generate resistance, misinformation and social fragmentation. Quarantine, safe burial protocols, movement restrictions, case investigation and surveillance may be epidemiologically justified, yet they can also reproduce histories of exclusion, coercion and institutional distrust.In many epidemic settings, frontline healthcare workers become the visible face of state authority and international response efforts. This places them in ethically complex positions as both caregivers and enforcers of public health interventions. The resulting tension can erode relationships between communities and health systems, particularly where previous experiences of neglect or political marginalisation remain unresolved.Community engagement should therefore be understood not merely as a communication strategy but as an ethical commitment grounded in respect, transparency and shared decision-making. Ethical engagement requires moving beyond transactional messaging towards genuine partnership with affected communities. This includes involving local leaders, women’s groups, faith-based organisations, youth representatives, survivors and traditional healers in planning and implementation.13Trust cannot be improvised during emergencies. It reflects longstanding relationships between institutions and communities. Epidemic responses that fail to acknowledge historical grievances risk deepening suspicion and undermining compliance. Ethical outbreak governance therefore depends on sustained investment in community-centred health systems long before crises emerge. Moral distress, institutional betrayal and workforce sustainabilityThe psychological consequences of epidemic response among frontline healthcare workers remain insufficiently addressed in global health preparedness frameworks. Repeated exposure to death, fear of infection, prolonged separation from family, stigmatisation and the emotional burden of triage decision-making contribute to moral distress and burnout. These experiences intensify when healthcare workers believe institutions have failed to provide adequate protection or support.A central ethical concern is the reciprocity deficit between healthcare systems and their workforce. During outbreaks, healthcare workers are frequently praised as heroes while working without adequate protective equipment, reliable salaries, psychosocial support, rest periods or safe working conditions. This disconnect creates a form of institutional betrayal: workers are expected to demonstrate extraordinary commitment while the systems that employ them fail to meet corresponding obligations.These conditions have implications beyond individual well-being. Workforce burnout undermines epidemic response capacity, weakens health system resilience and contributes to long-term attrition in already understaffed systems. Ethical preparedness must therefore include workforce sustainability as a central objective, not a secondary consideration.Health systems and international partners should institutionalise psychological support services, peer-support structures, adequate rest periods and occupational protections as standard components of outbreak response.14 Equally important is the need for visible institutional accountability. Health ministries and healthcare institutions should establish standing ethics preparedness structures linked to emergency preparedness committees, with clear authority to develop context-specific guidance on duty to care, workforce protection, triage, compensation, community engagement and psychosocial support. In other words, these structures would help make ethical decisions in the midst of changing circumstances, pressing deadlines, uncertainty and danger. Frontline healthcare workers and community representatives would be included in these structures and use transparent decision-making procedures as well as conduct periodic preparedness exercises so that ethical guidance is available before scarcity and uncertainty intensify during an emergency.9 13Implementation also requires durable ethics capacity rather than ad hoc consultation during crises. One practical model is the establishment of embedded empirical ethics networks within health and research systems.15 By identifying emerging ethical challenges in real time, supporting transparent decision-making during crises, documenting and addressing moral distress among frontline workers and facilitating community engagement and accountability, such networks can contribute directly to ethical preparedness. National governments retain primary responsibility for core health-system functions and should incorporate workforce protection, infection prevention, occupational health, psychosocial services and ethics preparedness into routine health and emergency budgets. However, where fiscal capacity is insufficient, regional bodies, bilateral and multilateral partners, global health security initiatives and research funders also have reciprocal responsibilities to provide predictable and additional support, particularly where outbreak control generates regional and global public goods.4 8 Funding arrangements should therefore move away from short-term emergency procurement towards multiyear preparedness financing, with explicit budget lines, transparent allocation criteria and accountability for whether promised protections reach frontline services.This approach does not eliminate the need for priority-setting. In severely constrained settings, not every preparedness measure can be implemented simultaneously. Governments and partners should therefore use transparent, participatory priority-setting to protect a minimum package of essential obligations first: reliable infection prevention and personal protective equipment, occupational protections and compensation, psychosocial support, fair triage processes and mechanisms for worker and community participation. full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionRecent outbreaks across Africa demonstrate that emerging infectious disease crises are not only biomedical events but recurring ethical and political stress tests for national health systems and global health governance. From West Africa to the DRC and East Africa, frontline healthcare workers have repeatedly been asked to confront extraordinary risks while operating within systems marked by inequity, scarcity and institutional fragility.The ethical dilemmas observed across Ebola, Marburg and COVID-19 responses show that epidemic preparedness cannot be reduced to surveillance systems, laboratory capacity and emergency containment strategies. Ethical preparedness, including workforce protection, transparent decision-making, reciprocal institutional obligations, psychosocial support and meaningful community engagement, must become central to global health security frameworks.Without sustained investment in resilient and equitable health systems, outbreaks will continue to place disproportionate moral and physical burdens on frontline healthcare workers. The true measure of preparedness is not only the capacity to contain outbreaks rapidly but also the ability of health systems to protect the dignity, safety and moral agency of the healthcare workers and communities expected to sustain the response. Embedded empirical ethics networks, integrated within health systems and research programmes, offer a promising mechanism for operationalising ethical preparedness.By building relationships, contextual knowledge and analytical capacity during interepidemic periods, such networks can support rapid, context-sensitive analysis of ethical trade-offs as well as ethical decision-making when crises emerge. As global health governance increasingly operates within a fractured global order, ethical preparedness cannot remain dependent on unstable cycles of outbreak response and short-term international solidarity. It must be embedded in the ordinary architecture of health systems before the next crisis begins.

Recurrent outbreaks of Ebola virus disease in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Uganda, alongside Marburg virus disease alerts in several African countries, show how rapidly localised epidemics can become regional and international public health threats.1 2 These crises reveal that high-consequence infectious disease outbreaks are not isolated national emergencies. They are interconnected global health challenges that expose structural inequities in preparedness, response and health system resilience.3 4These vulnerabilities are unfolding within a shifting international political and economic order. The move from aid-centred global health engagement towards the growing ‘prominence of trade objectives’ occurs in an increasingly fragmented geopolitical environment.5 While such transitions may create opportunities for economic advancement, they also risk deepening the vulnerability of health systems already strained by historical underinvestment, debt burdens, workforce shortages and uneven infrastructure development.6 Under these conditions, epidemic response capacity cannot be separated from broader questions of global justice and the distribution of institutional resilience.Recent Ebola outbreaks in the DRC and Uganda, together with recurring Marburg virus disease threats, continue to expose ethical and structural weaknesses in post-COVID-19 health systems. Even outbreaks that remain relatively contained impose substantial moral and occupational burdens on healthcare workers operating within fragile institutions.7 Across recurrent epidemics, the foundational pillars of resilient health systems—workforce capacity, infection prevention infrastructure, essential medicines, financing, governance and community trust—remain uneven and often inadequate.8 9Frontline healthcare workers are therefore required to navigate competing obligations to patients, families, colleagues, communities and themselves while often lacking adequate institutional protection. The ethical dilemmas they face extend beyond clinical decision-making. They include questions of professional duty amid personal risk, justice in resource allocation, reciprocity between institutions and workers, community trust and the psychological consequences of sustained moral distress.7 10 These challenges are amplified in contexts where historical neglect, underinvestment and inequitable global responses have eroded confidence in public institutions.This commentary argues that ethical preparedness must become a central component of epidemic response. Without transparent decision-making processes, reciprocal institutional support, and meaningful community engagement, outbreak responses risk collapsing under the weight of moral uncertainty, endangering both healthcare workers and the populations they serve. Ethical preparedness and the limits of the duty to careEmerging infectious disease outbreaks expose a fundamental tension within healthcare professionalism: the expectation that healthcare workers will continue delivering care despite substantial personal risk. During outbreaks of highly infectious diseases, frontline healthcare workers are expected to uphold beneficence while facing threats to their own safety, their families and their communities. Yet the ethical legitimacy of this expectation depends on whether institutions and governments fulfil reciprocal obligations to protect them.In many low-resource settings, this reciprocity remains incomplete. Similar patterns emerged during COVID-19, when health systems worldwide relied on professional altruism to compensate for chronic underinvestment in workforce protection. The repeated normalisation of healthcare worker sacrifice reveals a dangerous assumption within global health governance: that resilience can substitute for structural support.Ethical preparedness must therefore be understood as a core pillar of epidemic preparedness. Protecting healthcare workers requires more than emergency procurement once crises begin. It demands sustained investment in workforce safety, fair compensation, mental health services, safe working conditions, transparent institutional accountability and mechanisms for worker participation in planning and response. Without these safeguards, healthcare workers are left to absorb the moral and physical costs of systemic fragility. In fragile health systems, triage extends beyond clinical prioritisation and becomes a reflection of deeper structural inequities.
